original.acip: DE LTAR BYAS NA, ZAS SKOM NYID LA YOD PA'I SGRIB PA CAN GYI YI DVAGS KYIS LONGS SPYOD PA LA MA BRTZAMS KYI BAR DU BZA' BTUNG DNGOS YIN KYANG , DES LONGS SPYOD PAR BRTZAMS PA NA, ZAS DE'I RIGS 'DRA PHYI MA RNAG KHRAG TU SKYE BA YIN GYI, RNAG KHRAG TU SNANG BA'I SNANG BA TZAM GYIS BZA' BTUNG GI BYA BA BYED PA MA YIN TE, DE YIN NA LAS 'BRAS LA SKUR BA BTAB PAR 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR, DER THAL, DE LTA BU'I YI DVAGS KYIS LAS 'BRAS LA SKUR BA BTAB PAR 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR,
original.wylie: de ltar byas na, zas skom nyid la yod pa'i sgrib pa can gyi yi dvags kyis longs spyod pa la ma brtsams kyi bar du bza' btung dngos yin kyang , des longs spyod par brtsams pa na, zas de'i rigs 'dra phyi ma rnag khrag tu skye ba yin gyi, rnag khrag tu snang ba'i snang ba tsam gyis bza' btung gi bya ba byed pa ma yin te, de yin na las 'bras la skur ba btab par 'gyur ba'i phyir, der thal, de lta bu'i yi dvags kyis las 'bras la skur ba btab par 'gyur ba'i phyir
original.english: Given all this, consider craving spirits that have obstacles that relate to their food and drink itself. The food and drink there really is food and drink, until such time as the spirit starts trying to eat or drink it. When he does try to do so, then the continuum of the food into the next moment starts becoming pus and blood. It is not though that it is the simple appearance of something as pus and blood that could ever function as something to eat or drink. If this were the case, then the rules of karma and its consequences would have to be less that what they really are. And this is true, for if a craving spirit like this ever existed it would represent a failure of the laws of karma and its consequences.

original.english: Suppose moreover that there were no pus and blood out there to appear as the pus and blood, and suppose that the mere appearance of something looking like pus and blood could ever function as something to eat or drink. Well then, you would also have to be able to use a comb on the hair that appears on a porcelain sink to a person with cataracts. Well because, according to you, there is no pus and blood out there to appear as pus and blood; according to you, the mere appearance of something looking like pus and blood can provide all the functions of things that you eat and drink.

original.acip: GANG GI TSE GZHAN SKYE DGAG PA 'DI LA DON DAM GYI KHYAD PAR SBYOR BA YIN PA DE'I TSE, JI LTAR MIG NI RAB RIB CAN GYI SHES PAS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA DMIGS PAS, RAB RIB KYIS MA BSLAD PA'I SHES PA LA SKRA SHAD SOGS MI SNANG BA LA GNOD PA MIN PA

This state of mind cannot draw into question the way in which no strand of hair or the like ever makes its appearance to a state of mind which is not infected by such cataracts.

original.acip: DE'I DON NI DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON GZHAN LAS SHES PAR BYA BA MIN PAR GSUNGS PA'I 'GREL PA TSIG GSAL LAS, JI LTAR RAB RIB CAN DAG GIS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA'I NGO BO PHYIN CI LOG PA MTHONG BA NA, RAB RIB MED PAS BSTAN DU ZIN KYANG, RAB RIB MED PA LTAR SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA RANG GI NGO BO MA MTHONG BA'I TSUL GYIS, RTOGS PAR BYA BA JI LTAR GNAS PA BZHIN RTOGS PAR MI NUS KYI,

original.english: The point here is explained by A Clarification of the Verses, commenting upon statements that the meaning of suchness is not something that can be learned from others: Suppose that those with cataracts see, mistakenly, something with the nature of a strand of hair, or the like. Someone who has no such cataracts can explain the situation to them, but still they will not be able to stop themselves from seeing the thing as having the nature of a hair or the like. As such, we say that a person is unable to understand something in the same way it exists for someone who does understand the thing; but rather…

original.acip: ZHES RAB RIB CAN LA RAB RIB MED PAS SKRA SHAD MED DO ZHES BSTAN KYANG, RAB RIB MED PAS MTHONG BA 'DRA BA'I SKRA SHAD MED PA MI RTOGS PAR GSUNGS PAS, NYAN PA POS DE LTAR MA RTOGS KYANG SKRA SHAD MED PA MI RTOGS PA MIN NO,,

original.english: What this is saying is that a person who has no cataracts can say to a person who still does have them, “There's no strand of hair there!”—but the latter person will not be able to realize the lack of a hair there in the same way that the person with no cataracts sees this. original.english: Suppose then that—due to the fact that a person's eyes are infected with some cataracts—a person who possesses such optical defects looks into a cup of horn held in their hand (or any similar vessel for eating or drinking), and perceives there a strand of hair “or something of the like” (which words indicate anything similar perceived inside the cup; say, a fly or the like).

original.acip: SKRA SHAD DANG SBRANG MA SOGS YIN PAR NGO BO LOG PA GANG ZHIG RNAM PAR BRTAGS PA NA, DE BSAL BAR 'DOD NAS SNOD DE LA YANG DANG YANG DU BSGRE BZLOG BYED PA'I TSEGS THOB PAR RIG STE,
original.wylie: skra shad dang sbrang ma sogs yin par ngo bo log pa gang zhig rnam par brtags pa na, de bsal bar 'dod nas snod de la yang dang yang du bsgre bzlog byed pa'i tshegs thob par rig ste
original.english: When they think that they see something then, as different than it really is—when they see the hair or the fly or whatever it may be—then naturally they would want to get it out of the cup, and so it would be completely appropriate for them to go to the trouble of turning the cup upside down and knocking it against the table repeatedly, to get the unwanted thing out.

original.acip: MIG DAG PA'I RAB RIB MED PAS DE'I GAN DU PHYIN NAS, SKRA SHAD SOGS DE DAG NYID KYI BDAG NYID GZHI GANG DU MTHONG BA DER MIG GTAD KYANG SKRA SHAD KYI RNAM PA DE DAG MA DMIGS SHING, SKRA SHAD DE'I RTEN CAN TE KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS GANG YANG RTOG PAR MI BYED DO,,

original.english: And then suppose that a person with clear eyes—someone without any cataracts—walks over to this other fellow and looks down to the spot where the first person thought they saw one of those actual things: the strand of hair or the like.

original.english: This other person will naturally then want to clear up the misperception that the one with the cataracts is having, and will do their very best to say something to help them stop their mistake: “But look, actually there's no strand of hair there at all.” We could not though in this case say that the speaker was trying to deny a hair that was actually there.

original.acip: RAB RIB CAN GYIS MTHONG BA'I SKRA SHAD KYI DE KHO NA NYID NI, RAB RIB MED PAS MTHONG BA DE YIN GYI, RAB RIB CAN GYIS MTHONG BA DE MIN NO,,

original.english: The one who sees the real nature—the suchness—of the hair that the person with the cataracts perceives is the person without the cataracts; it is not in fact something that the person with the cataracts is capable of perceiving.

original.acip: ,SHES PAR BYED TSUL NI, MA RIG PA'I RAB RIB KYIS GNOD PA BYAS PA STE BLO BSLAD PAS DE KHO NA NYID MA MTHONG BA RNAMS KYIS, PHUNG PO DANG KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED LA SOGS PA'I RANG GI NGO BO DMIGS PA NI, PHUNG SOGS DE DAG GI NGO BO KUN RDZOB PA STE RAB RIB CAN GYIS SKRA SHAD DMIGS PA LTA BU'O,,

original.english: And just how should we accomplish this understanding? original.english: One may come then with the following argument: A person whose eyes are free of any cataracts doesn't perceive even the false appearance of a strand of hair. And that's simply because—if anything does in fact exist—then it has to be seen by an Enlightened Being. But if, on the other hand, the deceptive forms of the parts to a person and so on didn't exist at all, then there would exist no such thing as someone achieving enlightenment. And that in turn is because a person who first attains the Wish to achieve enlightenment for all living beings is someone who is still infected by misunderstanding.

original.acip: RAB RIB DANG BRAL BA'I MIG SHES LA, RAB RIB CAN LA SNANG BA'I SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA MED KYANG, SNANG BA DE MED MI DGOS PAS SANGS RGYAS DANG MI 'DRA'O,,

original.english: There is no such thing as something making its appearance as the strand of hair that appears to a person who has cataracts, as one which appears to a person whose visual consciousness is free of such cataracts. Nonetheless, it is not the case that the appearance would have to be something that did not exist; thus the case is different from that with an Enlightened Being.

original.acip: 'DIR GZUGS BRNYAN LAS NI DE 'DZIN PA'I MIG SHES SKYE BAR GSUNGS PAS, GZUGS BRNYAN DNGOS PO YIN ZHING SHES PA DANG NGO BO THA DAD PAS NI, PHYI ROL GYI DON YIN LA DE YANG MIG SHES KYI DMIGS RKYEN YIN PAS, GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DU BZHED PA YIN TE, ZLA GNYIS DANG SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA DANG SGYU MA SOGS DANG, SGRA BRNYAN SOGS LA YANG DE BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA'O,,

original.english: When this says that the visual awareness which grasps to a reflection has grown from a reflection, what it's saying is that the reflection itself is an actual thing, and that it is not such that to be the awareness of it is to be the reflection. As such, the reflection is an outside object, and is serving as an “object factor” for the arisal of the visual consciousness. Thus then the reflection is accepted here as belonging to the door of sense of visible form. You should understand appearances such as the doubled moon, and the hair in the sink—as well as illusions and echoes and the like—as being the same.

original.acip: DE LTAR NA DBANG SHES 'KHRUL PA LA SNANG BA'I BYAD DANG ZLA GNYIS DANG SKRA SHAD SOGS NI, DBANG PO LA 'PHRAL GYI GNOD PA MED PA'I SHES PA LNGA LA SNANG BA'I RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA DANG 'DRA'O,,

original.english: And so what's being said here is that when our sense perceptions are mistaken, and an object which is actually just a reflection in the mirror appears to us—or we see things like the two moons, or a hair lying there—it is similar to the case with our five sense perceptions when they are not affected by any adventitious defect, but things appear to them to exist by definition.

original.english: It's also like objects Equivalent in the way They're not really there; Those with cataracts Are sure they see Strands of hair, But other things That we don't even see. Similarly, You should understand That it's not as if What has ripened Will ripen once again.

original.acip: JI LTAR TE DPER NA YUL NI YOD PA NYID MIN PAR MTSUNGS BZHIN DU, RAB RIB CAN GYI MIG GIS YOD PA MIN PA'I SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA'I RNAM PAR NI MTHONG GI ,DE LAS GZHAN PA'I DNGOS PO'I RNAM PA BONG BU'I RVA DANG, MO GSHAM GYI BU LA SOGS PA'I RNAM PAR MTHONG BA MA YIN PA LTAR,

original.english: It's like, for example, how specific objects might be equivalent in the way that they are not really there. original.acip: RAB RIB CAN GYI MIG GIS SKRA SHAD SOGS MTHONG BA DANG, BONG BU'I RVA LA SOGS PA MI MTHONG BA'I NGES PA DE'I PHYIR RNAM SMIN YID DU 'ONG BA NI MI DGE BA LAS MI 'BYUNG LA, RNAM SMIN YID DU MI 'ONG BA NI DGE BA LAS MA YIN PA'I PHYIR, RNAM SMIN MI DGE BA STE YID DU MI 'ONG BA NI, NAG PO'I LAS LAS YIN LA, RNAM SMIN DGE BA STE YID DU 'ONG BA NI DGE BA LAS 'BYUNG BA YIN PAR MTHONG ZHING,

original.english: Eyes affected by cataracts see things like strands of hair; but it is definite that they do not see things like horns on top of the head of a rabbit. We can see then that a non-virtuous ripening—an unpleasant one—is something that comes from a black karma; while a virtuous ripening—a pleasant one—is something that comes from a good deed.

original.acip: DANG PO LA GNYIS, RMI LAM GYI DPE DGAG PA, SKRA SHAD MTHONG BA'I DPE DGAG PA'O,,

original.english: The first section comes in two steps of its own: denying the metaphor of a dream; and denying the metaphor of seeing a strand of hair.

original.acip: 'O NA RAB RIB CAN GYIS YOD PA MA YIN PA'I SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA DMIGS PA'I PHYIR, PHYI ROL MED KYANG RNAM PAR SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA YIN NO ZHE NA

original.english: One might come with the following: It is indeed the case that—even though there are no outer objects—awareness does exist through a nature of its own; this is due to the fact that a person who has cataracts on their eyes does perceive strands of hair and the like which do not actually exist.

original.acip: DE YANG MI 'THAD DO, ,CI'I PHYIR ZHE NA, MIG GI DBANG PO RAB RIB DANG BCAS PA LA BLO GANG GIS RAB RIB KYI MTHU LAS SKRA SHAD RNAMS GANG MTHONG BA NA,

original.english: This too though is a mistaken idea. And why is that? Let's think of a sense power of the eye which has cataracts; that is, when a particular state of mind sees certain strands of hair due to the influence of cataracts.

Relative though to the sight of someone who is seeing objects clearly—that is, to the sight of an eye which has no cataracts—both the appearance of something as a strand of hair and the state of mind which holds this appearance are false; which is to say, neither one has actually grown. That is, it would be difficult to say that one ascertained the existence of a state of mind if there were not even any object which was just appearing to be there.

original.english: As such, it is only a person who is experiencing the ripening of a deep seed that was planted by another, previous state of mind that possessed an image of a hair that will have an awareness arise with the image of a strand of hair.

original.acip: ,GANG GI PHYIR RAB RIB MED PAR YUL MTHONG BA DAG LA SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA'I BLO YI NUS PA BAG CHAGS NI SMIN PA MED PA DE'I PHYIR RAB RIB MED PA DE LA SKRA SHAD MTHONG BA'I BLO SKYE BAR MI 'GYUR BA YIN GYI, SHES BYA SKRA SHAD DU YOD PA'I DNGOS PO DANG BRAL BAS BLO DE MI SKYE BA MIN NO ZHE NA,

original.english: It is not however the case that there would be any ripening of a deep seed—the potential for a state of mind that took on the aspect of a strand of hair—with those who saw the object but had no cataracts. And for this reason then, it is not the case that a state of mind where they saw a strand of hair could ever come to grow with these individuals who had no cataracts. It is not though the case that this state of mind would fail to grow because it was devoid of any entity which possessed an existing object which was a strand of hair. Suppose then that this were your position. The present has no potential on its own

original.english: When a strand of hair makes its appearance to the consciousness of the eye it belongs, like a reflection in a mirror, to the sense door of visible form.

original.english: What this is indicating is that there is no difference between knowable things and the awareness which knows them, as far as existing through some nature of their own, or not. And what this is saying is that—if there is no strand of hair—then neither is there any state of mind which is taking that strand as its aspect. It is absolutely not the position of this master though to say that—if the object that one was thinking was there when we perceived a horse or cow in an illusion didn't really exist—then the state of mind that was grasping to it didn't exist either.

original.english: And thus we can say that consciousness could never be something—no matter which way you look at it—that could exist through some nature of its own. If you say that something exists only because it has an erroneous factor, then for the very same reason we'd have to say that if something lacked an erroneous factor, then it couldn't exist at all. original.english: It's possible For some people, By force of a cataract, To be made to hold, Mistakenly, A strand of hair, One moon as two, The pattern Of a peacock's feathers, A random fly, or Something of the like [f. 209b]. original.english: It's possible for ones sense powers to be skewed by force of the effects of a cataract; so that some people with cataracts may mistakenly see a strand of hair that's not actually there; or one moon that appears as two; or a spot of color like the pattern on a peacock's feathers; a random fly; or something of the like. original.english: And then we would have to ask you a question: Why is it that you would see things like that strand of hair that didn't exist; but not see this child of a barren woman?

Fruits from the examination

original.english: Suppose, for example, that we worked very hard to attack the idea—held by individuals who have cataracts on their eyes—that the strands of hair that they were seeing were either just one alone, or some great number, or somehow rounded, or black, or anything else of the like.

original.english: Denying the metaphor of seeing a strand of hair * * *

original.acip: CHU 'BAB KLUNG LA YI DWAGS RNAG BLO YANG ZHES SOGS KYI SKABS SU MTHA' DPYAD PA, LA CHU KLUNG RNAG KHRAG TU SNANG BA'I YI DWAGS KYI MIG SHES DANG BSE RU'I NANG DU SKRA SHAD 'DZAG PAR SNANG BA'I RAB RIB CAN GYI MIG SHES DANG SA GZHI KENG RUS KYIS KHYAB PAR SNANG BA'I KENG RUS GSAL SNANG CAN GYI TING NGE 'DZIN DANG BCAS PA RNAMS KYI YUL DE DANG DER YOD MED RNAM PA KUN DU MTSUNGS SAM MI MTSUNGS ZHE NA
original.wylie: chu 'bab klung la yi dwags rnag blo yang zhes sogs kyi skabs su mtha' dpyad pa, la chu klung rnag khrag tu snang ba'i yi dwags kyi mig shes dang bse ru'i nang du skra shad 'dzag par snang ba'i rab rib can gyi mig shes dang sa gzhi keng rus kyis khyab par snang ba'i keng rus gsal snang can gyi ting nge 'dzin dang bcas pa rnams kyi yul de dang der yod med rnam pa kun du mtshungs sam mi mtshungs zhe na
original.english: Here we will analyze the statement [from Entering the Middle Way, by Master Chandrakirti (650 AD)] where it says, "...The mind of a craving spirit as well, which sees a stream of water as pus." One may begin with the following question: Let's consider the objects of the following states of mind: the visual consciousness of a craving spirit where a river of water looks like pus and blood; the visual consciousness of a person with a kind of cataract where a clean white porcelain basin looks like a hair has fallen into it; and that kind of meditation where you visualize skeletons—where you imagine that the entire surface of the earth is covered with the bones of corpses. Are all these objects completely equivalent, as far as being something that exists or doesn't exist?

original.acip: KHO NA RE DE LTAR CIG CAR DU BLTAS PA'I TSE RNAG KHRAG DNGOS GNAS PA MED PAR, THAL RAB RIB CAN GYIS BSE RU LA BLTAS PA DE'I TSE BSE RU'I NANG DU SKRA SHAD MED PA GANG ZHIG RAB RIB DANG LDAN DBANG PO CAN MTSUNGS PA CHU 'BAB KLUNG LA YI DWAGS RNAG BLO YANG ZHES GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR ZER NA
original.wylie: kho na re de ltar cig car du bltas pa'i tshe rnag khrag dngos gnas pa med par, thal rab rib can gyis bse ru la bltas pa de'i tshe bse ru'i nang du skra shad med pa gang zhig rab rib dang ldan dbang po can mtshungs pa chu 'bab klung la yi dwags rnag blo yang zhes gsungs pa'i phyir zer na
original.english: Someone might make the following claim: Isn't it true that when all those beings sit down together and look at something, there isn't any actual pus and blood at all? Because isn't it true first of all that, when a person with cataracts looks into a porcelain basin, there is no strand of hair in the basin at all? And, secondly, doesn't [Master Dharmakirti's] text itself say, Identical to the case of someone where his sense power has a cataract, Is the mind of a craving spirit as well, which sees a stream of water as pus.

original.acip: RAB RIB CAN LA SKRA SHAD 'DZAG PAR RTOG PA'I GANG ZAG GI MIG LA SKRA SHAD SNANG GA LA DGOS, KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR RTOGS PA'I PHYIR RDZUN PA SGYU MA LTA BUR RTOGS PA YIN GYI, BDEN PAR KHAS BLANGS MI DGOS SO,,

original.english: Consider then a person who has a scratch on the surface of their eye, and who thus thinks they see a hair lying on the surface of their kitchen sink. How could you say then that a hair was appearing to their eyes? A person can perceive that things are deceptive-that they are like an illusion-because they have understood what deceptive reality is; but that doesn't mean they have to take it as real.

original.acip: DE NI RANG BZHIN MED PA RTOGS NA MIG DAG PA LA SKRA SHAD BZHIN DU SNANG BA MTHA' DAG NUB CING MA MTHONG BA'I SGO NAS RTOGS PA DANG,
original.wylie: de ni rang bzhin med pa rtogs na mig dag pa la skra shad bzhin du snang ba mtha' dag nub cing ma mthong ba'i sgo nas rtogs pa dang
original.english: What this line is actually saying though is that-when we realize that nothing has any nature of its own-it's like that hair on the sink for someone whose eyes are perfectly fine. That is, the appearance of the hair has faded away into nothing; we don't see the hair at all. And it's the same process here, for that realization.

original.acip: RAB RIB MED NA SKRA SHAD LDOG PAR MTHONG BA'I PHYIR RO,,
original.wylie: rab rib med na skra shad ldog par mthong ba'i phyir ro
original.english: After all, we can see that-when a cataract is removed from our eyes-we stop seeing hairs sticking to our white porcelain sink. No starting, no ending, no staying

original.acip: PHYIN CI LOG DANG PHYIN CI MA LOG PA DAG NI THA DAD PA YIN NO, ZHES PA NAS, [DE'I PHYIR, GANG GI TSE RAB RIB CAN GYIS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA LTAR PHYIN CI LOG GIS YOD PA MA YIN PA YOD PA NYID DU 'DZIN PA DE'I TSE NI YOD PAR GYUR PA'I DON CHA TZAM YANG DMIGS PAR GA LA 'GYUR,
original.wylie: phyin ci log dang phyin ci ma log pa dag ni tha dad pa yin no, zhes pa nas, [de'i phyir, gang gi tshe rab rib can gyis skra shad la sogs pa ltar phyin ci log gis yod pa ma yin pa yod pa nyid du 'dzin pa de'i tshe ni yod par gyur pa'i don cha tsam yang dmigs par ga la 'gyur
original.english: After all, a state of mind which is entirely mistaken is completely separate from one which is not mistaken in any way. We can for example look at a case where a person with cataracts on their eyes believes that there is a strand of hair lying on a white porcelain sink; they are certain that there is something there, when in fact there is nothing-they're just seeing a line on the eyeball itself. We could never say, in this instance, that there was present there even a tiny percentage of any actual object-any actual hair there.

original.acip: GANG GI TSE RAB RIB CAN MA YIN PAS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA LTAR PHYIN CI MA LOG PAS YANG DAG PA MA YIN PA SGRO MI 'DOGS PA DE'I TSE NA YANG GANG GIS NA DE'I TSE NA KUN RDZOB TU 'GYUR BA YOD PA MA YIN PAR GYUR PA'I DON CHA TZAM YANG DMIGS PA GA LA YOD,

original.english: And suppose another person comes along who has no cataracts on their eyes. They have none of this tendency for seeing a false object; one which simply isn't there-the hair or whatever it may be. And this is because their state of mind is one which is not mistaken. We could never say, again, that there was present there even a tiny percentage of any object which did not exist in a deceptive manner.

original.acip: SNYING GA'I THAD DU 'BAR 'DZAG SKRA SHAD 'DZINGS PA LTA BU LA SEMS GTOD NAS BUM CAN LA NAN TAN BYA,
original.wylie: snying ga'i thad du 'bar 'dzag skra shad 'dzings pa lta bu la sems gtod nas bum can la nan tan bya
original.english: Focus the mind onto this dripping and blazing tug-of-war at the heart area (which looks like a battle between single strands of hair), and make a concerted effort to hold the vase.

original.wylie: smad kyi me lce haM la phog pas de las byang sems dkar po skud pa ltar skya nar gyis babs pas smad kyi me rlung thur du mnan te, snying ga'i thad du 'bar 'dzag skra shad 'dzags pa lta bu la sems gtad pa dgos tshul sogs gsungs
original.english: At the end of this process, the flame of the fire of the lower half strikes the hang letter, and this makes the white element of enlightenment ooze down in a thin, elongated stream, like a long string.  This presses down upon the fire and wind of the lower half.
